question: Who sets the prices of phone calls, video visits and commissary items in prisons and jails, and can the facility or sheriff keep a commission?

gold_sections.why: State prisons (CDCR): voice calls must be free to the caller and the person called, and no state agency may receive revenue from voice or any other communication services, so there is no commission; CDCR has operational discretion so free calls do not interfere with necessary programming.

State prison canteens: the department maintains them, the Secretary specifies what is sold, and prices may not exceed a 35-percent markup over vendor cost (the version in force until January 1, 2028; the 2028 version has the Secretary fix self-supporting prices).

Net proceeds of state prison canteens go into the CDCR Inmate Welfare Fund, a trust held by the Secretary and used solely for the benefit and welfare of inmates (including canteen operations, staff and stock); each warden decides local use at least twice a year with inmate advocates and advisory council members.

County jails: the sheriff may run a jail store and fixes its prices (no markup cap); profits and any money, refund, rebate or commission from a telephone company or pay telephone provider for pay telephones primarily used by inmates go into the county inmate welfare fund, spent primarily for inmates; money not needed for their welfare may fund jail maintenance including program staff pay, but not required confinement costs except to augment them, with an itemized annual report to the board of supervisors; also covers non-sheriff county and city facilities.

Local jails: no charge for on-site in-person or video visits, no conversion from in-person to video-only, and video-only facilities must give on-site video and the first hour of remote video per week free.
The Public Utilities Commission's statutory role is service quality standards for incarcerated persons calling services in state and local facilities; the code sets no rates.
Newly booked arrestees get at least three completed calls free within the local calling area (two more for custodial parents), at their own expense outside it.
"Local detention facility" (used by 4032) means city, county, city and county or regional facilities confining adults, including contract facilities holding local prisoners, but not CDCR facilities.

nuggets.text: State prisons and CDCR youth facilities must provide voice calls free of charge to both the person calling and the person receiving the call.
nuggets.quote: shall provide persons in their custody and confined in a correctional or detention facility with accessible, functional voice communication services free of charge to the person initiating and the person receiving the communication

nuggets.text: No state agency may receive revenue from voice calls or any other communication services provided to people in state correctional or detention facilities, so the state takes no commission.
nuggets.quote: A state agency shall not receive revenue from the provision of voice communication services or any other communication services to a person confined in a state correctional or detention facility.

nuggets.text: The department must keep a canteen at each active prison or institution under its jurisdiction, and the Secretary of the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation specifies what it sells.
nuggets.quote: The department shall maintain a canteen at an active prison or institution under its jurisdiction for the sale to incarcerated persons of toilet articles, candy, notions, and other sundries, and shall provide the necessary facilities, equipment, personnel, and merchandise for the canteen. The secretary shall specify what commodities shall be sold in the canteen.

nuggets.text: Under the version in force now (until January 1, 2028), state prison canteen prices may not exceed a 35 percent markup above what the department paid its vendors.
nuggets.quote: The sale prices of the articles offered for sale shall not exceed a 35-percent markup above the amount paid to the vendors.

nuggets.text: Starting January 1, 2028, the markup cap ends and the Secretary fixes canteen prices at amounts that, as far as possible, make each canteen self-supporting.
nuggets.quote: The sale prices of the articles offered for sale shall be fixed by the secretary at the amounts that will, as far as possible, render each canteen self-supporting.

nuggets.text: All net proceeds from state prison canteens and hobby shops are deposited in the CDCR Inmate Welfare Fund.
nuggets.quote: There shall be deposited in the Inmate Welfare Fund all net proceeds from the operation of canteens and hobby shops

nuggets.text: Money in the CDCR Inmate Welfare Fund must be used solely for the benefit and welfare of people held in CDCR prisons and institutions, including setting up, staffing and stocking the prison canteens.
nuggets.quote: The money in the fund shall be used solely for the benefit and welfare of inmates of prisons and institutions under the jurisdiction of the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, including the following: (A) The establishment, maintenance, employment of personnel for, and purchase of items for sale to inmates at canteens maintained at the state institutions.

nuggets.text: Each county sheriff may establish and operate a store (commissary) in connection with the county jail.
nuggets.quote: The sheriff of each county may establish, maintain and operate a store in connection with the county jail

nuggets.text: The sheriff fixes the sale prices at the jail store, and any profit goes into an inmate welfare fund kept in the county treasury.
nuggets.quote: The sale prices of the articles offered for sale at the store shall be fixed by the sheriff. Any profit shall be deposited in an inmate welfare fund to be kept in the treasury of the county.

nuggets.text: Any money, refund, rebate or commission from a telephone company or pay telephone provider that is attributable to pay telephones primarily used by inmates must be deposited in the county inmate welfare fund, so the statute contemplates a jail receiving such a commission but routes it to that fund.
nuggets.quote: There shall be deposited in the inmate welfare fund any money, refund, rebate, or commission received from a telephone company or pay telephone provider when the money, refund, rebate, or commission is attributable to the use of pay telephones which are primarily used by inmates while incarcerated.

nuggets.text: The sheriff must spend inmate welfare fund money primarily for the benefit, education and welfare of the people held in the jail.
nuggets.quote: The money and property deposited in the inmate welfare fund shall be expended by the sheriff primarily for the benefit, education, and welfare of the inmates confined within the jail.

nuggets.text: A local jail may not charge for visits when the visitor is on site, whether the visit is in person or by video.
nuggets.quote: A local detention facility shall not charge for visitation when visitors are onsite and participating in either in-person or video visitation.

nuggets.text: A jail that offered only video visitation as of January 1, 2017 must offer on-site video visits free and, if it offers remote video visits, the first hour per week free.
nuggets.quote: If a local detention facility offered video visitation only as of January 1, 2017, on-site video visitation shall be offered free of charge, and the first hour of remote video visitation per week shall be offered free of charge if the facility offers remote video visitation.

nuggets.text: The California Public Utilities Commission must set service quality standards that communication providers serving state or local correctional or detention facilities must follow.
nuggets.quote: The commission shall establish service quality standards for incarcerated persons calling services to be adhered to by communication service providers rendering services to state or local correctional or detention facilities.

nuggets.text: A newly booked arrestee may make at least three calls free if they are to numbers in the local calling area, and at the arrestee's own expense outside it.
nuggets.quote: The arrested person shall be entitled to make at least three calls at no expense if the calls are completed to telephone numbers within the local calling area or at his or her own expense if outside the local calling area.

nuggets.text: Inmate welfare fund money not needed for inmates' welfare may be spent on maintaining county jail facilities, which can include the salaries and benefits of staff who run programs for inmates.
nuggets.quote: Any funds that are not needed for the welfare of the inmates may be expended for the maintenance of county jail facilities. Maintenance of county jail facilities may include, but is not limited to, the salary and benefits of personnel used in the programs to benefit the inmates

nuggets.text: The inmate welfare fund may not pay the county's required costs of confining inmates, such as meals, clothing, housing or medical care, except to augment those costs when the sheriff decides that is in inmates' best interests.
nuggets.quote: Inmate welfare funds shall not be used to pay required county expenses of confining inmates in a local detention system, such as meals, clothing, housing, or medical services or expenses, except that inmate welfare funds may be used to augment those required county expenses as determined by the sheriff to be in the best interests of inmates.

nuggets.text: The sheriff must submit an itemized report of inmate welfare fund expenditures to the board of supervisors every year.
nuggets.quote: An itemized report of these expenditures shall be submitted annually to the board of supervisors.

nuggets.text: A local jail that offered in-person visits as of January 1, 2017 may not convert to video visitation only.
nuggets.quote: A local detention facility that offered in-person visitation as of January 1, 2017, may not convert to video visitation only.

nuggets.text: CDCR has operational discretion in carrying out the free-call rule so that free voice calls do not interfere with necessary programming.
nuggets.quote: The Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation shall have operational discretion in implementing this subdivision such that free voice communication services do not interfere with necessary programming.

nuggets.text: For a county adult detention facility not run by the sheriff, the board of supervisors designates the county official who takes the sheriff's store and fund duties, and for a city jail, city officials take those duties.
nuggets.quote: the board of supervisors shall designate the proper county official to exercise the duties otherwise allocated in this section to the sheriff. (g) The operation of a store within any city adult detention facility shall be governed by the provisions of this section, except that city officials shall assume the respective duties otherwise outlined in this section for county officials.

nuggets.text: Each prison warden, with at least two inmate advocacy group representatives and two inmate advisory council members, meets at least twice a year to decide how Inmate Welfare Fund money is used at that institution.
nuggets.quote: The warden of each institution, in collaboration with at least two representatives from local or state advocacy groups for inmates and two members of either the men's or women's advisory council or similar group within each institution, shall meet at least biannually to determine how the money in the fund shall be used to benefit the inmates of the respective institution.

office.value: State prisons: the Secretary of the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation decides what the canteen sells (and, under the version that later replaces the markup cap, fixes canteen prices); voice calls are free by statute
County jails: the sheriff runs the jail store and fixes its sale prices (no statutory markup cap)
County adult facilities not under the sheriff: the county official the board of supervisors designates; city jails: city officials
California Public Utilities Commission: service quality standards (not prices) for incarcerated persons calling services

amount.value: State prison canteen prices: no more than a 35 percent markup above the amount paid to vendors (version in force today)

yes_no.value: State prisons: no, no state agency may receive revenue from voice or any other communication service. County jails: no California statute bars it, but any money, refund, rebate or commission from a telephone company or pay telephone provider for pay telephones primarily used by inmates must go into the inmate welfare fund, be spent primarily for inmates, may fund jail maintenance including program staff pay only when not needed for inmates' welfare, and may not pay required confinement costs except to augment them (federal FCC site-commission rules are outside the state code)

answer: California's code sets few prices; most call, video and vendor rates come from contracts and regulators. In state prisons, voice calls are free to both parties [N1]. No statute prices video calls or messaging, but no state agency may take communication revenue, so no commission [N2]. The department runs prison canteens and the Secretary decides what they sell [N3]; markups are capped at 35% over vendor cost [N4] until January 1, 2028, when the Secretary sets self-supporting prices [N5]. Net proceeds go to the Inmate Welfare Fund [N6], used only for prisoners, including running canteens [N7]. In county jails, the sheriff may run a store [N8], fixes its prices with no markup cap, and deposits profits in a county inmate welfare fund [N9] (a supervisor-designated official or city officials act at other jails [N21]). No California statute bans jail phone commissions: payments from phone providers for pay phones used mainly by inmates go into that fund [N10], spent primarily on inmates [N11]; surplus may maintain the jail, including program staff pay [N16], but not cover required costs like meals or medical care, only add to them [N17]. No statute addresses jail video, tablet or commissary vendor commissions; a 2024 FCC order banned call and video site commissions, though later orders revised its terms and deadlines. Jails may not charge for on-site visits [N12] or switch from in-person to video-only [N19]; video-only jails as of 2017 must give a free remote hour weekly [N13]; other remote video prices are contractual.

out_of_corpus.what: Caps on the rates and ancillary fees providers may charge for interstate and intrastate audio and video calls from prisons and jails, and site commissions: the FCC's 2024 incarcerated communications order (FCC 24-75) prohibited providers from paying site commissions to correctional facilities on audio and video calling services, which goes beyond anything in the California code; later FCC orders have revised rate caps and compliance dates, so check the current order
out_of_corpus.where: FCC incarcerated people's communications services rules, 47 CFR Part 64 Subpart FF, adopted under 47 U.S.C. 276 as amended by the Martha Wright-Reed Just and Reasonable Communications Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117-338); FCC WC Docket Nos. 23-62 and 12-375

out_of_corpus.what: Intrastate rate caps, ancillary fee limits and service quality standards for incarcerated persons calling services in California jails, set under the Commission's general authority over telephone corporations and Public Utilities Code 2899
out_of_corpus.where: California Public Utilities Commission decisions in its incarcerated persons calling services rulemaking (R.20-10-002 and successor proceedings)

out_of_corpus.what: Actual per-minute call rates in county and city jails, remote video visit and messaging prices, tablet and deposit fees, any commission percentage paid to a county, and commissary vendor prices
out_of_corpus.where: Each county's (sheriff's or board of supervisors') contracts with phone, video, tablet and commissary vendors, and CDCR's statewide communication and canteen vendor contracts (public records under the California Public Records Act)

out_of_corpus.what: Rules on prison telephone use, visiting (including video visits), canteen operations and inmate trust accounts in state prisons
out_of_corpus.where: California Code of Regulations, Title 15, Division 3 (CDCR), and the CDCR Department Operations Manual

out_of_corpus.what: Minimum standards for telephone access, visiting and inmate welfare fund and commissary administration in local detention facilities
out_of_corpus.where: Board of State and Community Corrections minimum standards for local detention facilities, California Code of Regulations, Title 15, Division 1, Chapter 1, Subchapter 4

out_of_corpus.what: Each jail's commissary price list, how the sheriff spends the inmate welfare fund, and the annual itemized expenditure report to the board of supervisors
out_of_corpus.where: County sheriff's office, county inmate welfare fund committee or commission where one exists, and board of supervisors records (Penal Code 4025(e))

version_flags: Cal. PEN § 5005: the version amended by Stats. 2023, ch. 609 (SB 474), effective January 1, 2024, with the 35-percent markup cap, is in force until it is repealed on January 1, 2028; the version amended by Stats. 2024, ch. 56 (AB 1875), operative January 1, 2028, drops the cap, has the secretary fix prices to make each canteen self-supporting, and adds sulfate-free shampoos and conditioners, curl creams and gel to canteen items.
Cal. PEN § 4025(a): commencing January 1, 2028, a jail store established by the sheriff must sell sulfate-free shampoos and conditioners, curl creams, and gel.
local_option: Each sheriff decides whether to run a jail store and fixes its sale prices, and decides how inmate welfare fund money (store profits and phone commissions, refunds and rebates) is spent primarily for inmates, reporting annually to the board of supervisors (Penal Code 4025); for a county adult facility not under the sheriff, the board of supervisors designates the county official, and for a city jail city officials take those duties (4025(f), (g)). Jail phone and remote video rates and any commission percentage are set in each county's vendor contracts, subject to CPUC and FCC rate rules.
notes: Two regimes. State prisons (CDCR): Penal Code 2084.5 (Keep Families Connected, SB 1008 of 2022) makes voice calls free to both parties and bars any state agency from receiving revenue from voice or any other communication service, which rules out commissions on calls, video visits, messaging and tablets; no statute sets a price for CDCR video visits or messaging, and the department has operational discretion over implementation. Canteens: 5005 (department maintains canteens, secretary specifies commodities, 35-percent markup cap until 2028, Department of Finance biennial audit, statements posted at the canteen and library) and 5006 (net proceeds to the Inmate Welfare Fund, a trust held by the secretary; uses include canteen operations, education, recreation, family visiting services; the warden meets at least biannually with advocates and inmate advisory council members to decide local use). 5006.1 bars certain IWF uses (overtime, TV repair and sets). Government Code 11013 (state-department canteens on a nonprofit basis) does not apply where a store is authorized by other law, as 5005 does for CDCR. County and city jails: 4025 lets the sheriff run a store and fix prices with no markup cap; profits, 10 percent of hobbycraft sales and telephone commissions, refunds and rebates (the text speaks of pay telephones primarily used by inmates) go to the county inmate welfare fund; funds go primarily to inmates' benefit, education and welfare, surplus may fund jail maintenance including program staff, but not required county confinement costs such as meals, clothing, housing or medical care except to augment them; itemized annual report to the board of supervisors. No California statute bans a county from receiving a phone commission or caps jail call rates, and none addresses commissions on jail video, tablet, messaging or vendor-run commissary contracts; the federal FCC 2024 order (FCC 24-75) prohibited site commissions on audio and video calling, with caps and compliance dates revised by later orders (see out_of_corpus). 4032 governs jail video visitation price only for on-site visits (free) and for facilities that were video-only on January 1, 2017 (on-site video free, first hour of remote video per week free); 4032(b) bars a facility that offered in-person visits on that date from converting to video-only; otherwise remote video prices are set by contract. 851.5 gives booked arrestees at least three free local calls (two more for custodial parents arranging child care), with a misdemeanor for willful denial. PUC 2899 gives the CPUC only service quality standards by statute; the CPUC's intrastate rate caps rest on its general ratemaking authority and are outside this corpus. Juvenile facilities are outside the question: Welfare and Institutions Code 208.1 makes voice calls free and bars county or city agencies from communication-service revenue in county or city youth facilities; WIC 873 (juvenile hall store, chief probation officer fixes prices, Ward Welfare Fund) and WIC 1752.5 (state youth canteen on a nonprofit basis) follow the older model. Penal Code 6401 requires CDCR emergency calls and video calls when an incarcerated person is hospitalized, without addressing price.
